title: Theseus apud Acheloum. Perimele
titleEn: Theseus at the Hall of Achelous; Perimele — Metamorphoses VIII.547–610
source: P. Ovidius Naso, Metamorphoses, ed. Hugo Magnus (Gotha: F.A. Perthes), public domain; TEI from PerseusDL/canonical-latinLit phi0959.phi006.perseus-lat2, sha256 fb3fdb1d8a4a3b82. Collated against The Latin Library (cltk mirror) as a disagreement detector only. Original spelling kept. Pronunciation convention: reconstructed Classical (restored) Latin, applied consistently. All translations were made fresh from the Latin for Lectorium.
about: Theseus, his share of a common labour discharged, is on the road to Athens when the Achelous — swollen with rain — closes the road and offers his own hall instead. Over dinner in a grotto of pitted pumice and shell, Theseus looks out at the water and asks what the land lying offshore is, and the river answers in his own voice: the Echinades were naiads once, who held a country sacrifice and left him out of it, and whom his flood tore loose and rolled into the sea. He then points out one island lying apart from the rest, Perimele — a girl whose maidenhood he took, and whose father threw her from a cliff for it; she was still swimming when new earth closed round her. Achelous is a river and a god at once throughout these lines, and the Latin moves between the two without warning: the same subject blocks a road as water and plays host as a person, and says intumui, “I swelled,” of rage and of rain in one word.

advisory.lede: This part contains a rape: the river-god Achelous, telling the story himself at his own table, says in a single line that he took the maidenhood of a girl named Perimele, and that her father then threw her from a cliff into the sea.
advisory.more: Ovid gives the act a single verse, VIII.592, and gives it to the god who committed it, speaking in his own voice at his own dinner table. The verb is one of taking away — the word Latin uses for confiscation — the girl is called “beloved,” and nothing whatever is said of her wish. What follows is punishment falling on her rather than on him: her father hurls her from a rock into the sea to die, and she ends the part as an island. The Latin is presented unaltered; the translation keeps the euphemism the god chooses and does not soften what it stands for.

sentences.t:
Interea Theseus sociati parte laboris
functus Erechtheas Tritonidos ibat ad arces.
sentences.l: Meanwhile Theseus, having performed his share of the shared toil, was going to the Erechthean heights of Tritonis.
sentences.i: Meanwhile Theseus, his part in the shared labour done, was making his way towards the Erechthean citadel of Tritonian Minerva.
sentences.n: functus is the participle of a deponent verb — active in meaning, passive in form — and it governs the ablative parte: “having discharged his share.” The share is of sociati laboris, the labour worked at in company. Tritonidos is a Greek genitive of Tritonis, a cult title of Minerva; Erechtheas arces names the citadel of Athens after Erechtheus, one of the city's earliest kings. Between them the two names say “the Athenian acropolis” without ever naming Athens.

sentences.t:
Clausit iter fecitque moras Achelous eunti
imbre tumens.
sentences.l: Achelous closed the road and made delays for him as he went, swelling with the rain.
sentences.i: Achelous, swollen with rain, blocked his road and held him up on his way.
sentences.n: Here is the doubleness that runs through the whole part and has to be felt once to be read at all: Achelous is a river in flood (imbre tumens, “swelling with the rain”) and a god who will speak in the next breath, and Latin marks no change between the two. One subject shuts a road as water and offers a roof as a host. eunti is a dative present participle of eo, “for him as he went” — the traveller is grammatically the person inconvenienced, not the person stopped.

sentences.t:
“Succede meis,” ait “inclite, tectis,
Cecropida, nec te committe rapacibus undis:
sentences.l: “Come under my roof,” he says, “illustrious one, son of Cecrops, and do not commit yourself to the snatching waves:
sentences.i: “Come in under my roof,” he said, “illustrious son of Cecrops, and do not trust yourself to these grasping waters.
sentences.n: meis ... tectis is a dative after succede, split around ait and the vocative inclite — the interlaced order that makes a Latin invitation formal. Cecropida is a Greek vocative patronymic, “descendant of Cecrops,” Athens' first king: a courteous way of saying “Athenian” to a man on his way there. rapacibus is the adjective built on rapio, “snatching,” the standing word for water that carries things off, and it prepares everything the next four lines describe.

sentences.t:
ferre trabes solidas obliquaque volvere magno
murmure saxa solent.
sentences.l: they are wont to carry solid beams and to roll rocks aslant with a great roaring.
sentences.i: these waters commonly carry off whole tree-trunks and send boulders tumbling sideways with a great roar.
sentences.n: The subject is still undae from the line before: solent, “they are accustomed,” governs two infinitives, ferre and volvere. trabes is a beam or baulk of timber, here a whole trunk torn from the bank. obliqua is an adjective agreeing with saxa, not an adverb with the verb — the rocks go slantwise as they roll, which English can only say adverbially, “aslant.” magno murmure is an ablative of manner straddling the line end, with murmure landing only after the turn — the noise reaches the ear after the rocks are already moving.

sentences.t:
Vidi contermina ripae
cum gregibus stabula alta trahi: nec fortibus illic
profuit armentis, nec equis velocibus esse.
sentences.l: I have seen high steadings bordering on the bank dragged off, herds and all: nor there did it profit to be strong cattle, nor swift horses.
sentences.i: I have seen tall byres at the water's edge carried away with the herds inside them, and there it was no help to be a strong ox or a fast horse.
sentences.n: vidi governs an accusative and infinitive, stabula ... trahi, “steadings being dragged.” contermina takes the dative ripae, “bordering on the bank.” In the second half profuit is impersonal — it has no personal subject, and the sense is “it was of no use” — and it is completed by the infinitive esse; fortibus armentis and equis velocibus stand in the dative because the unexpressed subject of esse has been attracted into the case profuit governs. English wants “to be a strong ox”; Latin says it in the dative.

sentences.t:
Multa quoque hic torrens nivibus de monte solutis
corpora turbineo iuvenalia flumine mersit.
sentences.l: Many a youthful body too, with the snows loosed from the mountain, has this torrent sunk in its whirling flood.
sentences.i: This torrent too, when the snows come loose from the mountain, has drowned many a young body in its whirling water.
sentences.n: nivibus de monte solutis is an ablative absolute, a self-contained “with the snows loosed from the mountain” where English wants a clause. quoque here is the ordinary adverb “also” — worth checking, because the same letters are often quo-que, “and so that,” as they are at line 579. The adjective multa waits a whole line for its noun corpora, and iuvenalia is added later still, so that the age of the drowned arrives last. Magnus prints flumine, “in its whirling stream”; some editions print vertice, “in its whirling eddy.” The subject is hic torrens either way, so the water that drowns is the speaker's own on both readings. torrens, “the torrent,” is the host naming himself in the third person one line after offering his roof.

sentences.t:
Tutior est requies, solito dum flumina currant
limite, dum tenues capiat suus alveus undas.”
sentences.l: Rest is safer, until the streams run in their accustomed channel, until their own bed holds slight waters.”
sentences.i: It is safer to wait until the streams run in their usual course, until the channel can hold water as slight as it should be.”
sentences.n: dum with the subjunctive (currant, capiat) means “until,” with a shade of purpose in it: wait for the time when. solito ... limite is an ablative of route split across the line end, the noun arriving only after the turn. tenues undas, “slight waves,” is the exact opposite of everything he has just described, and suus alveus, “their own bed,” quietly makes the flood a trespass.

sentences.t:
Adnuit Aegides, “utar” que “Acheloe, domoque
consilioque tuo” respondit; et usus utroque est.
sentences.l: The son of Aegeus nodded, and “I shall use,” he answered, “Achelous, both your house and your counsel”; and he used both.
sentences.i: Theseus nodded, and answered, “Achelous, I will take both — your house and your advice”; and he took both.
sentences.n: Aegides is a patronymic, “son of Aegeus,” that is, Theseus; Acheloe is the Greek vocative. utor, the deponent utar (active in sense despite its shape), takes the ablative, so domo and consilio are not objects but ablatives, and the verb returns at the end of the line as the perfect usus est. The repetition is the point: he says he will use both, and the narrator confirms in three words that he did. The enclitic -que is printed outside the closing quotation mark, hanging on the quoted utar from without, because the connective belongs to the narrator's sentence and not to the words Theseus speaks.

sentences.t:
Pumice multicavo nec levibus atria tophis
structa subit: molli tellus erat umida musco,
summa lacunabant alterno murice conchae.
sentences.l: He goes in under halls built of many-hollowed pumice and of tufa not smooth: the ground was damp with soft moss, shells panelled the topmost parts with alternating murex.
sentences.i: He passed into a hall built of pitted pumice and rough tufa; the floor was damp with soft moss, and shells panelled the ceiling in alternating bands of purple.
sentences.n: nec levibus tophis is litotes — “tufa not smooth” for stone deliberately left rough, the taste of a grotto rather than a house. subit is “goes in under,” which is what one does with a cave rather than a hall. lacunabant is built on lacunar, a coffered ceiling: the shells themselves are doing the panelling, and alterno murice describes the purple of the murex shell laid in alternating courses. The tenses shift from present (subit) to imperfect (erat, lacunabant) as the narrative stops walking and starts looking.

sentences.t:
Iamque duas lucis partes Hyperione menso
discubuere toris Theseus comitesque laborum:
sentences.l: And now, with Hyperion having measured off two parts of the daylight, they reclined on the couches — Theseus and the companions of his labours:
sentences.i: And now, two parts of the daylight measured off by Hyperion, Theseus and his companions in that labour took their places on the couches:
sentences.n: discubuere is discubuerunt: the poetic third-plural perfect in -ere, which returns again in this part at instruxere, posuere and duxere. Hyperione menso is an ablative absolute whose participle, from the deponent metior, is active in sense — “Hyperion having measured,” not “having been measured.” Hyperion is the Sun; two of the day's three parts gone puts the hour well past midday, at the Roman dinner hour.

sentences.t:
hac Ixionides, illa Troezenius heros
parte Lelex, raris iam sparsus tempora canis,
quosque alios parili fuerat dignatus honore
amnis Acarnanum, laetissimus hospite tanto.
sentences.l: on this side the son of Ixion, on that side the Troezenian hero, Lelex, now sprinkled as to his temples with a few grey hairs, and whatever others the river of the Acarnanians had deemed worthy of like honour, most delighted at so great a guest.
sentences.i: on one side Ixion's son, on the other the hero of Troezen, Lelex, his temples by now flecked with a little grey — and any others the Acarnanian river had held worthy of the same honour, overjoyed as he was at so great a guest.
sentences.n: hac and illa are both ablatives waiting for parte, which is held back to the start of the next line, so the two sides are named before the word “side” arrives. Ixionides is Pirithous, son of Ixion; the Troezenian hero is Lelex, placed by his city rather than his father. sparsus tempora canis is the Greek accusative of respect: tempora, “temples,” is an accusative saying in what respect he is sprinkled — “sprinkled as to his temples” — with canis the ablative of the grey hairs themselves. The construction returns three lines below. dignatus fuerat is a pluperfect of the deponent dignor, active in sense, “had thought worthy.” amnis Acarnanum, “the river of the Acarnanians,” is the narrative naming the host by his water even as he plays host: Achelous is the boundary river of Acarnania.

sentences.t:
Protinus adpositas nudae vestigia nymphae
instruxere epulis mensas dapibusque remotis
in gemma posuere merum.
sentences.l: At once nymphs, bare as to their feet, laid the tables set beside them with the courses, and, the feast removed, set out unmixed wine in a jewel.
sentences.i: At once nymphs, barefoot, furnished the tables drawn up beside the couches with the courses; and when the meal was cleared they poured the unmixed wine into jewelled cups.
sentences.n: nudae vestigia is the same Greek accusative of respect met at line 568: the nymphs are “bare as to the soles of their feet.” instruxere and posuere are again the third-plural perfect in -ere. dapibus remotis is an ablative absolute, “the courses having been taken away.” merum is wine unmixed with water, so the phrase marks the drinking that follows the eating rather than the meal itself; in gemma is a singular standing for the plural, jewelled cups.

sentences.t:
Tum maximus heros,
aequora prospiciens oculis subiecta, “quis” inquit
“ille locus?” digitoque ostendit, “et insula nomen
quod gerit illa, doce: quamquam non una videtur.”
sentences.l: Then the greatest hero, looking out over the level waters lying below his eyes, says, “What is that place?” and pointed with his finger, “and tell me what name that island bears: although it does not seem one.”
sentences.i: Then the greatest of the heroes, looking out over the water spread below him, said, “What is that place?” — and pointed — “and tell me what name that island carries, though it does not look like a single one.”
sentences.n: aequora ... subiecta oculis is “the level waters lying under the eyes,” with oculis a dative after the compound sub-icio. The quotation is broken twice by narrative, first by inquit, then by digito ostendit, which is how a speech is kept inside a scene rather than lifted out of it. doce is an imperative, “teach me,” a shade more formal than “tell me,” and it is what turns the guest into a listener. The closing clause, non una videtur, is the observation the whole answer will be built on.

sentences.t:
Amnis ad haec “non est” inquit “quod cernitis, unum:
quinque iacent terrae: spatium discrimina fallit.
sentences.l: The river to this says, “What you are looking at is not one thing: five lands lie there; the distance cheats the divisions.
sentences.i: To this the river said, “What you are looking at is not one. Five lands lie there; the distance hides what separates them.
sentences.n: ad haec, “to this,” is the standing formula for introducing a reply. The predicate unum is held to the very end of its clause, so the denial arrives only after the reader has already accepted the oneness. discrimina are the gaps that divide one island from the next; the subject of fallit is spatium, and it is the distance that does the deceiving, not the islands. Achelous answers as a landlord who knows his own delta — and as the water that made it.

sentences.t:
Quoque minus spretae factum mirere Dianae,
naides hae fuerant.
sentences.l: And that you may wonder the less at the deed of slighted Diana, these had been naiads.
sentences.i: And so that you may wonder the less at what slighted Diana did — these were naiads once.
sentences.n: Quoque here is quo-que, “and so that,” not the adverb “also” that it was at line 556: quo with a comparative (minus) and the subjunctive mirere makes a purpose clause, “so that you may wonder the less.” Read quoque twice whenever a subjunctive follows it. mirere is mireris with the alternative second-person ending -re for -ris, common in verse, from the deponent miror, active in sense. spretae Dianae is a genitive with factum: the deed is Diana's, and the participle spretae, “slighted,” carries the whole motive in one word.

sentences.t:
Quae cum bis quinque iuvencos
mactassent rurisque deos ad sacra vocassent,
inmemores nostri festas duxere choreas.
sentences.l: And when they had slaughtered twice five bullocks and had called the gods of the countryside to the rites, unmindful of us they led the festal dances.
sentences.i: And when they had sacrificed ten young bulls and called the country gods to the offering, they led out the festal dances with no thought of me.
sentences.n: Quae is a connecting relative opening the sentence — “and they,” not “which” — one of the commonest ways Latin ties a new sentence to the last. mactassent and vocassent are the syncopated pluperfect subjunctives mactavissent and vocavissent, ordinary in verse. bis quinque, “twice five,” is the epic way of counting ten. inmemores nostri takes an objective genitive, and nostri is the plural of majesty, so it means “forgetful of me.” The offence is precise: they summoned the gods of the fields and left out the water that feeds them.

sentences.t:
Intumui, quantusque feror, cum plurimus umquam,
tantus eram,
sentences.l: I swelled up, and as great as I am carried along when at my fullest ever, so great was I,
sentences.i: I rose in flood; as great as I ever run at my highest, so great I was —
sentences.n: feror is fero in its passive form used of moving water, “I am carried along,” the ordinary Latin for a river in spate — and the river is saying it of himself. quantus ... tantus is a correlative pair, “as great as ... so great,” with the qualifying clause cum plurimus umquam, “when at my most ever,” folded inside it. This is where the god and the water are least separable: intumui, “I swelled,” is what a man does with rage and what a river does with rain, and the Latin does not choose.

sentences.t:
pariterque animis inmanis et undis
a silvis silvas et ab arvis arva revelli
cumque loco nymphas, memores tum denique nostri,
in freta provolvi.
sentences.l: and monstrous alike in temper and in waters, I tore woods from woods and fields from fields, and rolled the nymphs, together with their ground — mindful of us then at last — into the sea.
sentences.i: and savage alike in spirit and in flood, I tore woodland from woodland and field from field, and rolled the nymphs, their ground with them, into the sea — mindful of me then, at last.
sentences.n: animis and undis are ablatives of respect after inmanis, and they state the doubleness outright: one adjective covers the god's temper and the water's violence at once, with no seam between them. a silvis silvas et ab arvis arva sets the same noun on both sides of each preposition, so the tearing sounds repetitive and mechanical. revelli and provolvi are first-person perfect actives, from revello and provolvo, not the present infinitives they resemble. memores ... nostri answers inmemores nostri at line 582, and the answer is bitter: they remembered him at the moment it could do them no good.

sentences.t:
Fluctus nosterque marisque
continuam diduxit humum partesque resolvit
in totidem, mediis quot cernis Echinadas undis.
sentences.l: Our wave and the sea's drew the continuous ground apart and loosed it into as many pieces as the Echinades you see amid the waters.
sentences.i: The wave — mine and the sea's together — pulled the unbroken ground apart and broke it into just as many pieces as there are Echinades you can see out in the water.
sentences.n: The doubled -que in nosterque marisque is the poetic “both ... and,” and noster is the plural of majesty again, so one flood belongs to the river and the sea at once. totidem ... quot is a correlative pair, “as many ... as,” which makes the count of the islands the measure of the damage. The Echinades are the small islands lying off the mouth of the Achelous on the western coast of Greece, and Echinadas keeps the Greek ending of its accusative plural. The whole tale is an aetiology: the river explaining a real archipelago outside his own door.

sentences.t:
Ut tamen ipse vides, procul en procul una recessit
insula, grata mihi; Perimelen navita dicit.
sentences.l: Yet, as you yourself see, far off — look, far off — one island has drawn away, dear to me; the sailor calls it Perimele.
sentences.i: But as you can see for yourself, one island stands well apart — there, far out — and it is dear to me; sailors call it Perimele.
sentences.n: The repeated procul en procul puts the pointing hand into the verse: en is a bare “look.” recessit is the perfect of recedo, used of something that moved off once and has stayed there since. navita is the older poetic form of nauta, “sailor,” and the singular stands for the class — what sailors call it, as against what Achelous calls it. Perimelen keeps its Greek ending -en in the accusative.

sentences.t: Huic ego virgineum dilectae nomen ademi.
sentences.l: From her, my beloved, I took away the name of maiden.
sentences.i: I took her maidenhood from her, and she was dear to me.
sentences.n: adimo means to take away from, and it governs the dative of the person deprived: huic ... dilectae, “from her, beloved.” virgineum nomen, “the name of maiden,” is a euphemism, but the verb beneath it is not one — nothing here is given, something is removed, and the participle dilectae records only what the taker felt. This one line is all these lines say about the act itself; everything after it is consequence, and the consequence falls on her.

sentences.t:
Quod pater Hippodamas aegre tulit inque profundum
propulit e scopulo periturae corpora natae.
sentences.l: Her father Hippodamas bore this ill, and from a crag pushed into the deep the body of his daughter, about to perish.
sentences.i: Her father Hippodamas took it hard, and pushed his daughter from a cliff into the deep, to her death.
sentences.n: Quod is another connecting relative, “and this,” and it is the object of tulit; aegre ferre is a fixed idiom, “to take badly.” periturae is the future participle of pereo attached to natae — “his daughter who was going to perish” — so the grammar announces the outcome before the fall happens. corpora is a poetic plural for one body, and what the line pushes off the rock is corpora natae, the body of his daughter, rather than the daughter herself.

sentences.t:
Excepi nantemque ferens “o proxima mundi
regna vagae” dixi “sortite, tridentifer, undae,
sentences.l: I caught her up and, carrying her as she swam, I said, “O you who have drawn by lot the realms next after the sky, the realms of the roaming wave, trident-bearer,
sentences.i: I caught her, and holding her up as she swam I said, “Trident-bearer, you who drew by lot the kingdom next after the sky, the kingdom of the roaming water,
sentences.n: sortite is the vocative of the deponent participle sortitus, active in sense, “having drawn by lot”: it points to the division of the universe among the three brothers, in which the sea fell to Neptune. mundus here is the heavens, Jupiter's share, and not “the world” in the wider sense, so proxima mundi regna is “the realms next after the sky” — second, not first, and the god being asked a favour is reminded of it. tridentifer, “trident-bearer,” is the kind of compound epithet Latin builds for gods. nantem has no noun with it: the object is simply “her, swimming.”

sentences.t:
adfer opem mersaeque precor, feritate paterna
da, Neptune, locum; vel sit locus ipsa licebit.”
sentences.l: bring help, and to her, sunk by a father's savagery, grant, I pray, Neptune, a place; or — it will be allowed — let her herself be a place.”
sentences.i: bring help; grant a place, Neptune, I beg you, to the girl her father's savagery has plunged beneath the sea — or, if it may be, let her herself be the place.”
sentences.n: adfer and da are imperatives with precor dropped between them, the way a Roman prayer inserts its own verb of praying inside the request. mersae is a dative with da, “grant to her who has been sunk”: mergo is to dip or plunge under, and she is still swimming two lines above, so the word says she has been put in the water, not yet that she has died in it. feritate paterna is the ablative of the cause that put her there, the father's savagery. The last clause turns on licebit, a future impersonal “it will be allowed,” used almost as a conjunction; sit is a jussive subjunctive, so the sense is “granted that, let her herself be a place.” The request is exact and strange: not that she be saved, but that she be turned into ground. The numbering jumps at this line, from 596 to 601, because the edition of record deletes 597–600 as interpolated — verses it judges not to be Ovid's — while keeping their numbers in its lineation. Nothing has fallen out of the text and nothing is supplied: the prayer runs on unbroken from 596 into 601.

sentences.t:
Dum loquor, amplexa est artus nova terra natantes,
et gravis increvit mutatis insula membris.
sentences.l: While I speak, new earth embraced her swimming limbs, and a heavy island grew upon her changed members.
sentences.i: Even as I speak, new earth closed about her swimming body, and a heavy island grew upon her altered limbs.
sentences.n: Dum loquor keeps the present with dum, “while I am speaking,” which Latin does even inside a past narrative: the change is made to happen inside the prayer, before it is finished. amplexa est is a deponent perfect, active in sense, with terra as its subject — the earth does the embracing. increvit is in-cresco with the dative mutatis membris, “grew upon her changed members”; artus in the line before and membra here are the poem's two words for the same body, varied rather than repeated. The numbering jumps again before this unit, from 602 to 609, for the same reason as at 601: the edition of record deletes 603–608 as interpolated and keeps their numbers. Between the two deletions, that is why this part carries 54 lines of the range VIII.547–610 and not 64 — nothing of the archived text is missing. gravis, “heavy,” agrees with insula, and it is the last thing said of what was, one line earlier, a girl swimming.
